metadata.title: Assessment of student ICT competence according to mathematics, science, and reading literacy: evidence from PISA 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 Turkey data with a two-stage stratified sampling design. To account for unequal probabilities of selection, the authors apply the final student weight W_FSTUWT in all analyses. For uncertainty estimation, they use the modified balanced repeated replication (BRR) approach, which is appropriate for PISA’s stratified multistage design and also incorporates plausible-value imputation error. The paper does not indicate any deliberate omission of weights; instead, it explicitly states that W_FSTUWT and BRR are used to handle the complex survey design and PV-related variance.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports plausible-value (PV) handling for PISA literacy scores (10 plausible values with pooling using Rubin’s combination criteria) and uses BRR to account for imputation error. However, it does not describe a specific missing-data strategy for questionnaire items or derived ICT scale indicators (e.g., whether cases with missing ICT items were excluded or imputed). Given the focus on secondary PISA public data and the reported outlier removal, this omission is a reporting gap for missingness handling beyond PV imputation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analyses are based on PISA 2018 Turkey students aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months in grade 7 or above (N=6890). The authors remove univariate and multivariate outliers from the Turkish sample, resulting in 5438 students for the factor analysis/correlation/SEM analyses. The ICT constructs are operationalized using the PISA 2018 ICT Familiarity Questionnaire derived variables (availability, ICT use, interest & perceived competence, and subject-related ICT use), and literacy outcomes are represented using PISA plausible values for mathematics, science, and reading.

main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM path coefficients (standardized β): AVB_ICT→MATH β=-0.13 (t=-8.88, p=0.00); ENT_USE→MATH β=-0.14 (t=-14.39, p=0.00); INTPER_ICT→MATH β=0.10 (t=101.46, p=0.00); USE_SCH→MATH β=0.10 (t=155.88, p=0.00); SUB_ICT→MATH β=0.23 (t=91.60, p=0.00). Model fit: RMSEA=0.07, CFI=0.93 (Model 1).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Turkey (grade 7+), the study leveraged ICT availability, entertainment ICT use, ICT interest and perceived competence, educational ICT use at school, and subject-related ICT use to predict mathematical literacy (PISA plausible values), finding that ICT availability and entertainment use had negative effects while ICT interest/competence, educational use, and subject-related use had positive effects. This indicates that policies should prioritize supporting purposeful, curriculum-linked ICT use and students’ ICT confidence rather than simply increasing access or entertainment-oriented use, while noting that the study is correlational and based on SEM with PVs.

main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM path coefficients (standardized β): AVB_ICT→SCIE β=-0.14 (t=-8.14, p=0.00); ENT_USE→SCIE β=-0.08 (t=-0.90, p=0.00); INTPER_ICT→SCIE β=0.11 (t=117.55, p=0.00); USE_SCH→SCIE β=0.10 (t=179.12, p=0.00); SUB_ICT→SCIE β=0.23 (t=100.21, p=0.00). Model fit: RMSEA=0.08, CFI=0.92 (Model 2).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Turkey (grade 7+), the study leveraged ICT availability, entertainment ICT use, ICT interest and perceived competence, educational ICT use at school, and subject-related ICT use to predict science literacy (PISA plausible values), finding that ICT availability and entertainment use had negative effects while ICT interest/competence, educational use, and subject-related use had positive effects. This indicates that science achievement may benefit more from students’ confident, educationally oriented ICT engagement than from access alone or entertainment use, though the evidence remains non-causal due to the observational SEM design.

main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM path coefficients (standardized β): AVB_ICT→READ β=-0.15 (t=-10.12, p=0.00); ENT_USE→READ β=-0.13 (t=-14.63, p=0.00); INTPER_ICT→READ β=0.16 (t=135.50, p=0.00); USE_SCH→READ β=0.09 (t=203.20, p=0.00); SUB_ICT→READ β=0.16 (t=86.74, p=0.00). Model fit: RMSEA=0.08, CFI=0.92 (Model 3).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Turkey (grade 7+), the study leveraged ICT availability, entertainment ICT use, ICT interest and perceived competence, educational ICT use at school, and subject-related ICT use to predict reading literacy (PISA plausible values), finding that ICT availability and entertainment use had negative effects while ICT interest/competence, educational use, and subject-related use had positive effects. This indicates that reading outcomes may improve when ICT is used for educational purposes and when students develop ICT confidence, rather than when ICT use is primarily entertainment-driven, while recognizing that causality cannot be inferred from SEM correlations.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 Turkey data (students in grade 7 or above; N=6890, with 5438 retained after univariate and multivariate outlier removal) to validate a four-dimensional ICT competence construct and to examine how ICT variables relate to mathematics, science, and reading literacy. ICT constructs are measured via Likert-type questionnaire-derived indices (availability, ICT use, interest & perceived competence, and subject-related ICT use), while literacy outcomes use PISA plausible values pooled across 10 PVs using Rubin’s combination criteria and estimated with BRR for the complex survey design. Using SEM path models with ESCS as a control/moderator, the authors report acceptable model fit (e.g., CFI≈0.92–0.93; RMSEA≈0.07–0.08) and find negative associations for ICT availability and entertainment use, alongside positive associations for educational ICT use, ICT interest/competence, and subject-related ICT use. Limitations include the non-causal, correlational nature of SEM and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling beyond PV imputation.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is not an empirical machine-learning prediction paper: the study uses factor analysis, correlation analysis, and structural equation modeling (SEM) with plausible values and survey-weighted variance estimation (W_FSTUWT and BRR). Therefore, no ML algorithms are evaluated, and ml_techniques.all_techniques is intentionally empty. The main findings are reported as SEM path coefficients and model-fit indices rather than ML predictive performance.
